name_en: He Huan Shan High Mountain Oolong
processing: Very lightly oxidised (around 10–15%), ball-rolled and dried without roasting, in the standard high-mountain style.
harvest_season: A late-spring pick in June and a winter pick in October; yields are low and some gardens manage only one good crop.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, dark bluish-green balls with short stems, compact and heavy.
appearance_liquor: Pale greenish gold, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Small, thick, deep-green leaves with little red at the edges, opening slowly over the first steeps.
taste_profile: Cool and sweet, with high florals, a hint of pine and a light, clean body a touch leaner than Li Shan, finishing with a long, clear aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Full dose, boiling water, a longer first steep to open the balls, then short steeps. Best in the first five or six infusions; very long steeps do not add much.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest, the June and October picks of the current year, in vacuum-sealed 75 g or 150 g packs and priced close to Li Shan. Quantities are modest, so treat plentiful or cheap 'He Huan Shan' as an altitude claim to be checked. It is drunk fresh, within a year of picking.
description:
He Huan Shan is a 3,400-metre massif on the Nantou–Hualien border, far above the tea line, and the oolong that carries its name grows on the road up to it: gardens in Ren'ai Township, Nantou, around Cui Feng and the Hehuanshan highway at roughly 1,700 to 2,200 metres. The name is partly marketing by proximity, but the gardens are genuinely high, cold and remote, and the tea belongs with Li Shan rather than Alishan in character.

It is Qing Xin oolong, lightly oxidised, ball-rolled and unroasted. The growing conditions are harsh even by high-mountain standards, with winter frost and a short growing season, so yields are low and the leaf is small and thick. The cup is cool and sweet, with high florals, a hint of pine and a light, clean body that is a touch leaner than Li Shan, with a long, clear aftertaste.

Brew it as you would any top high-mountain tea: full dose, water off the boil, a longer first steep to open the balls, then short steeps and patience. It is at its best in the first five or six infusions and does not reward pushing with very long steeps.

It is sold by harvest, a late-spring pick in June and a winter pick in October, in vacuum-sealed packs, and priced close to Li Shan. The name is used elastically, so treat 'He Huan Shan' as an altitude claim to be checked: ask for the garden and the altitude, and expect a modest quantity, not a container-load.

Try it against a Li Shan lot from the same season to see how much a few valleys can change the same cultivar.
history:
This is a trade name borrowed from the Hehuan massif rather than a tea from its summit: the gardens lie lower down, in the Ren'ai area of Nantou. Which gardens qualify is loosely defined, and little is documented about when tea was first planted there.

It belongs to the wave of Taiwanese high-mountain oolong and is usually spoken of in the same breath as Li Shan.
